title: Inclusive education: supporting learners with special needs under CBE
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals on identifying and supporting learners with special educational needs in ways that fit CBE and the realities of ordinary schools.
body:
CBE is built on the idea that every learner can demonstrate competence in their own way. For learners with disabilities or learning difficulties, that principle only becomes real if the school notices needs early and adapts what it does.

Most of this does not require specialist equipment. It requires attention, small adjustments, and the right partners.

Identify needs early

Ask at admission about any disability, health condition, or learning difficulty, and record what parents say. Teachers are often the first to notice that a learner cannot see the board, struggles to hear, or finds reading unusually hard. Create a simple way for teachers to flag these concerns to the school.

Where your sub-county has an Educational Assessment and Resource Centre, refer learners there for proper assessment and advice.

Practical adaptations that make a difference

  • Seating that suits the learner, such as near the front or away from noise.
  • Extra time and a quiet space for assessments where appropriate.
  • Large print, clear handwriting, and materials in accessible formats.
  • Breaking tasks into smaller steps and giving clear, repeated instructions.
  • Assessment methods that let the learner show competence in ways other than writing.

Adjustments are not lower standards: Extra time or a different format changes how a learner shows what they know. It does not change what they are expected to know. Explain this to staff and parents to avoid resistance.

Support the teachers

Teachers need basic guidance on common conditions and on how to adapt lessons. A short session, perhaps using the holiday development window, goes a long way. Pair teachers with colleagues who have experience.

Think about access

Check ramps, doorways, toilets, and classroom layout for learners with physical disabilities. Small changes made at low cost, such as a handrail or a reserved ground-floor classroom, can be decisive.

Work with parents and protect dignity

Parents know their child best and should be partners in planning. Keep information confidential, and talk about support and strengths, not labels. Make it clear to all students that differences are respected.

Keep learner support information organised and private.
